lead: This unit explains how light is generated in optical transmitters, how it is launched into fiber, and how joints and modulators affect the link. After it, you can choose between an LED and a laser diode for a given link, estimate coupled power and joint loss, and read a Mach-Zehnder modulator transfer curve.
about: Unit 3 moves from light-matter basics to complete transmitter hardware. Chapter 3.1 defines absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission, the three processes behind every optical source. Chapter 3.2 turns spontaneous emission into practical LEDs: planar, dome, surface and edge emitters, with efficiency and modulation limits. Chapter 3.3 adds feedback and population inversion, giving the threshold condition for laser oscillation. Chapter 3.4 applies it to semiconductor laser diodes; chapter 3.5 covers heterojunction and quantum-well designs. Chapter 3.6 calculates source-to-fiber power launching, while chapter 3.7 treats fiber joints, connectors and misalignment loss. Chapter 3.8 closes with external modulation and Mach-Zehnder devices, connecting the transmitter to WDM links in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Light interacts with atoms by absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission; the last two differ in whether a second photon triggers the emission.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at full depth. Cover photon energy E=hf, two-level atoms, absorption, spontaneous lifetime τ_sp, stimulated emission, Einstein A and B coefficients, B12=B21, A21=(8πhf³/c³)B21, population ratio, and why stimulated emission needs an inverted population.

figure.aria: A tree groups absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission under light-atom interaction, with short notes on the photon change in each.

chapters.example: An atom has spontaneous lifetime τ_sp = 5 ns at λ = 850 nm. Find the photon energy in eV and the Einstein A coefficient. If the excited-state population is twice the ground-state population, state whether net stimulated emission or absorption dominates. Use h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s, 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
chapters.trap: Thinking spontaneous emission needs a second photon; it does not. Also A is a rate per second, not an energy.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: photon energy and basic atomic energy levels.
chapters.leave: Laser cavity design to 3.3; semiconductor band structure to 3.4–3.5; detector absorption to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An LED is a forward-biased p-n junction that emits spontaneous light; its structure and efficiencies decide how much power leaves the chip and enters the fiber.
chapters.depth: Cover direct-bandgap recombination, planar LED, dome LED, surface emitter LED and edge emitter LED; some syllabi call the surface emitter a Burrus LED. Cover internal quantum efficiency, extraction efficiency, external efficiency, power efficiency, I-P curve, emission spectrum, modulation bandwidth and temperature effects.

figure.aria: A tree groups LED structures into surface emitters, with planar and dome variants, and edge emitters.

chapters.example: A planar LED has internal quantum efficiency 0.70, extraction efficiency 0.20 and current 50 mA. Photon energy is 1.4 eV. Find the external optical power. Use 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.
chapters.trap: Do not multiply by extraction twice; external efficiency already includes internal quantum efficiency and extraction. Keep current in amperes for watts.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 spontaneous emission; Unit 1 numerical aperture for later coupling.
chapters.leave: Laser action to 3.3–3.5; source-fiber coupling formulas to 3.6.

chapters.idea: Laser action needs gain from population inversion, optical feedback from a cavity, and enough pump to cross a threshold gain.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the full derivation. Cover metastable level, N2>N1, gain coefficient, Fabry-Perot cavity, round-trip gain equals loss, threshold condition Γg_th = α_i + (1/(2L))ln(1/(R1R2)), longitudinal modes and threshold current.

figure.title: Laser conditions
figure.aria: Block diagram of a laser: pump creates inversion, the gain medium is fed back by mirrors, and output leaves through a partial mirror.

chapters.example: A Fabry-Perot semiconductor laser has L = 300 μm, R1 = R2 = 0.32, internal loss α_i = 10 cm⁻¹ and confinement factor Γ = 0.30. Find the threshold modal gain and threshold material gain.
chapters.trap: Mixing centimetres and metres in mirror loss; forgetting that Γ multiplies material gain; using R instead of R1R2.
chapters.leave: Semiconductor laser construction to 3.4; quantum wells to 3.5; direct modulation to 3.8.

chapters.idea: A semiconductor laser diode is a forward-biased p-n diode whose cleaved facets form a Fabry-Perot cavity, giving coherent output above a threshold current.
chapters.depth: Cover double-heterostructure active region, injected carriers, spontaneous emission, carrier recombination, stimulated emission, cleaved facet mirrors, threshold current density, L-I curve, slope efficiency, longitudinal and transverse modes, temperature dependence and direct modulation. Some syllabi call it an injection laser diode (ILD).

figure.aria: Plot of laser output power against current: zero below 20 mA threshold, then a straight line with slope 0.3 mW per mA.

chapters.example: A laser diode has threshold current 20 mA and slope efficiency 0.30 W/A. Find output power at 40 mA and 60 mA. At 60 mA, the forward voltage is 1.8 V; find electrical power and efficiency.
chapters.trap: Using total current instead of (I − I_th) for output; slope efficiency has units W/A, not W.
chapters.leave: Heterojunction and quantum-well details to 3.5; coupling to 3.6; modulation schemes to 3.8.

chapters.idea: Heterojunctions confine carriers and light to a small active region; quantum wells add size-quantised energy levels and lower threshold current.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover double heterostructure, separate confinement heterostructure, quantum well, multiple quantum well, strained quantum well, bandgap and refractive-index steps, carrier confinement, optical confinement, threshold reduction and wavelength shift. Mention DFB and DBR only as feedback variants.

figure.aria: Layer stack of a quantum-well laser: p and n AlGaAs cladding surround a thin GaAs active layer on a GaAs substrate.

chapters.example: A GaAs quantum well is 10 nm wide. The electron effective mass is 0.067m0. Find the lowest confined electron energy above the band edge. Use h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s and m0 = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg.
chapters.trap: Putting the well width in nanometres directly into the formula; the energy varies as 1/L², so width errors matter.
chapters.prereq: 3.3–3.4 threshold and laser diode; Unit 1 waveguides.
chapters.leave: DFB design and WDM lasers to Unit 6; detailed band structure to solid-state physics.

chapters.idea: Only a fraction of source power enters a fiber; coupling efficiency depends on source radiance, fiber numerical aperture, core area and alignment.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the full calculation. Cover direct coupling from LED and laser, radiance, numerical aperture, coupling efficiency, Fresnel reflection, lens coupling, tapered fiber, pigtailing and alignment tolerance. Use η≈NA² for a small Lambertian LED and η≈(r_core/r_source)²NA² when the source area is larger.

figure.title: Source coupling
figure.aria: Block diagram of source-to-fiber coupling: light from the source passes through a lens to the fiber face and becomes a guided mode.

chapters.example: A Lambertian LED has emitting-area radius 100 μm. A step-index fiber has core radius 50 μm and NA = 0.20. Total LED power is 2.0 mW. Assume the source area is larger and uniform. Find the coupled power.
chapters.trap: Using NA instead of NA², or forgetting the area mismatch; dB is a ratio, not a power.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 LED emission; Unit 1 numerical aperture and modes.
chapters.leave: Fiber-to-fiber joints and connectors to 3.7; link power budget to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Every joint or connector loses light through lateral, angular and longitudinal misalignment, plus core and NA mismatch; loss is best handled in dB.
chapters.depth: Cover fusion splice, mechanical splice and connector; intrinsic loss from core diameter, NA and refractive-index difference; extrinsic loss from lateral offset, angular tilt, end separation, end finish and Fresnel reflection. Include connector names SC, ST and LC, return loss, and the lateral-offset overlap formula for step-index multimode fiber.

figure.aria: A tree separates joint loss into intrinsic causes such as core size and NA, and extrinsic causes such as lateral, angular and gap misalignment.

chapters.example: Two step-index multimode fibers have core radius a = 50 μm and NA = 0.22. A lateral offset d = 10 μm is the only misalignment. Estimate coupling efficiency and loss in dB.
chapters.trap: Adding dB losses of two joints by multiplying fractions; convert each fraction to dB and add. Also use d/(2a), not d/a, in the overlap formula.
chapters.prereq: 3.6 coupling; Unit 1 numerical aperture and core radius.
chapters.leave: Link power budget to Unit 5; WDM couplers to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An optical modulator changes the amplitude or phase of light after the laser; a Mach-Zehnder interferometer converts a phase change into an intensity change.
chapters.depth: Cover direct modulation limits, external modulation, electro-optic effect, phase modulation, Mach-Zehnder interferometer, push-pull drive, transfer function P_out/P_in = cos²(Δφ/2), Vπ, extinction ratio, insertion loss, chirp and electro-absorption modulators. Some syllabi call the device a Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM).

figure.title: Mach-Zehnder modulator
figure.aria: Block diagram of a Mach-Zehnder modulator: input light splits into two arms, each arm gets a phase shift, and the combiner produces output interference.

chapters.example: A push-pull Mach-Zehnder modulator has Vπ = 4 V. Input optical power is 2.0 mW. The phase difference is Δφ = πV/Vπ. Find output power at V = 2.0 V and at V = 4.0 V.
chapters.trap: Using P ∝ cos(Δφ) instead of cos²(Δφ/2); forgetting that Vπ is the voltage for a π phase shift.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 laser diode; Unit 1 waveguide modes; Unit 6 WDM application.
chapters.leave: Receiver detection to Unit 4; full WDM network to Unit 6; driver electronics to lab.
